items.title: NBTI announces $600m pipeline for Nigerian innovation
items.description: By Luminous Jannamike ABUJA — The National Board for Technology Incubation (NBTI) has unveiled an investment and development-finance pipeline exceeding $600 million for solar energy and other development initiatives, following the participation of 298 Nigerian innovators at the NextGen Innovation Challenge 2026 in London. The proposed financing comprises a $500 million solar-energy programme for universities and polytechnics and a $100 million financing arrangement for the Tinubu Light Initiative. The funds, however, have not been confirmed as received or fully mobilised. Speaking at a world press conference on Wednesday, NBTI Director-General, Dr Kazeem Kolawole Raji, said the October 9 event, organised in partnership with UKALD, provided an international platform for showcasing Nigerian technologies and connecting innovators with investors and commercial partners. The number of participating innovators rose from 105 in 2025 to 298 this year, representing all 36 states and the Federal Capital Territory, with innovations spanning agriculture, healthcare, artificial intelligence, renewable energy and advanced manufacturing. “Our innovators have demonstrated that Nigeria has ideas worthy of international attention. Our responsibility is to help create the conditions in which those ideas can grow, compete and deliver lasting value to our people,” Raji said. NBTI said discussions with Gigawatt Global focused on developing solar farms in universities and polytechnics under power purchase agreements, while a memorandum of understanding with Financial Innovation for Impact, UK, also known as Cambridge Investors, covered the proposed $100 million financing for the Tinubu Light Initiative. The initiative targets one million micro and small businesses for solar-energy solutions, 50,000 direct youth jobs and 10,000 trained field marketers, with ₦30 billion in blended financing targeted for its first phase. Other outcomes include an announced $100,000 investment commitment by Dubai-based investor Erin Grover for three women innovators and international acceleration opportunities valued at $160,000 for 16 selected innovators. The Learning and Development Bureau UK also offered leadership and management scholarships worth more than £80,000 collectively to the 16 innovators and pledged assistance with UK Global Talent Visa applications, subject to eligibility. Raji said the priority was now to turn the opportunities into viable businesses, jobs and measurable economic benefits, urging investors and development partners to support Nigerian innovators with funding, mentorship and market access. “Our focus must now move decisively from visibility to implementation, from promising concepts to commercially viable solutions, and from announcements to independently verifiable outcomes,” he said. items.title: Who protects the dreamer? (Part II) — Reflections on the vulnerability of the Girl Child in the Obuasi Senior High Technical School Scandal
items.description: By Thelma Takyiwaa Ankomah There is something sickeningly cruel about a society that encourages a girl to dream, sends her to school to build that dream, and then leaves her vulnerable to the very people entrusted with protecting her. The allegations emerging from Obuasi Senior High Technical School against its headmaster, Zakaria Abdulai, involving sexual abuse, including rape, are deeply disturbing. If established, these allegations would represent not merely a crime, but a monstrous betrayal of trust, authority and the sacred responsibility of educating children. I am angry. Deeply angry. And every Ghanaian who cares about the safety of our children should be furious. What makes this matter particularly horrifying is the power imbalance between a school authority and the students placed under his care. A school should be a sanctuary of learning, not a place where a girl must fear the person who ought to protect her. I strongly encourage everyone to watch “ Inside the dreaded headmaster’s bungalow” By Manasseh Azure Awuni – JoyNews on this scandal. Watch it with an open mind, but prepare yourself emotionally. The revelations are deeply disturbing, and you may find yourself asking how such allegations could emerge from an institution entrusted with the future of young people. You will be angry. You will be troubled. And you will understand why silence, indifference and institutional complacency are unacceptable. When the protector becomes the subject of allegations A headmaster is entrusted with authority, not given a licence to intimidate, exploit or abuse. That position exists to protect students, not expose them to danger. We must ask the hard questions. Were complaints previously made? Who received them? Who acted, and who looked away? Were warning signs ignored? Did anyone use influence, position or political connections to suppress concerns? If institutional failures occurred, those responsible must be identified and held accountable. Ghana cannot afford another theatrical investigation in which committees are established, press statements are issued, and eventually everybody returns to business as usual. Enough of the hypocrisy. Enough of the institutional cowardice. Enough of treating the suffering of vulnerable children as a public-relations inconvenience. Where is the ministry responsible for protecting our girls? The Ghana Education Service, the Ghana Police Service, the Attorney-General’s Department and the Ministry of Gender, Children and Social Protection must demonstrate urgency, competence and moral courage. Madam Agnes Naa Momo Lartey, protecting children cannot be a ministerial title displayed on an official website. It must be demonstrated when girls are allegedly violated and the nation demands answers. Where is the visible, forceful advocacy for these girls? Where is the unmistakable demand for their protection, counselling, dignity and justice? This is not the time for timid statements or bureaucratic excuses. It is time to stand firmly with vulnerable children and insist that every relevant institution does its job. No political shields. No selective justice. The NDC’s statement of 20th October 2026 calling for Mr Abdulai to step aside to facilitate an unhindered investigation was welcome. But the circumstances surrounding the matter also demand scrutiny of how concerns were handled. Political affiliation must never become a protective shield. Neither should public outrage become a substitute for evidence. The presumption of innocence must be respected, but due process must not be weaponised to justify inaction. Who protects the dreamer? Red Wednesday must become more than wearing red for photographs and social media attention. It must become a national revolt against the normalisation of abuse, the protection of powerful individuals and the abandonment of vulnerable girls. If the allegations are proven, justice must be uncompromising. If officials failed in their duties, they must answer. If institutional weaknesses enabled abuse, they must be exposed and corrected. Our girls are not bargaining chips. Their dignity is not negotiable. Their futures must never be sacrificed to protect powerful people, political parties or institutional reputations. No cover-ups. No excuses. No selective accountability. No investigation as usual. Justice for our girls. Protect the dreamer. No cover-ups. No selective accountability. No investigation as usual. Justice for our girls, without fear or favour. #RedWednesday #ProtectTheGirlChild #JusticeForOurGirls #InstitutionalAccountability #NoOneIsAbovmeTheLaw

items.title: Obuasi SHTS students remain at home nearly 3 months after closure over headmaster’s sexual abuse claims
items.description: The academic future of many second-year and final-year students of Obuasi Senior High and Technical School (SHTS) remains uncertain, as the school has been closed to continuing students for nearly three months. The school was shut down on August 5 following an order by the municipal assembly after a riot in which students reportedly attacked the headmaster, Zakaria Abdulai, over allegations of sexual abuse involving female students. Despite the commencement of the new academic year for senior high schools, academic activities at Obuasi SHTS have yet to resume for continuing students. JoyNews checks in the mining town revealed that some second-year and final-year students were helping with domestic chores, while others were engaged in trading activities, with no clear indication of when they would return to the classroom. Anthony Coffie, president of a group known as Concerned Citizens of Adansi, has expressed concern over the situation and called for the students to be allowed to return to school. “The situation is particularly alarming for Form Three students, who should be preparing intensively for their West African Senior School Certificate Examination (WASSCE). The loss of valuable instructional time threatens their examination preparation and academic prospects,” he said. Mr Coffie said students should not be made to suffer the consequences of what he described as an administrative crisis, stressing the need to protect their right to education. “Our children must not become collateral victims of an administrative crisis. Their right to education and their prospects for academic success must not be sacrificed while the relevant authorities deliberate over the issues surrounding the school,” he said. He is appealing to the Adansihene to engage the government, the Minister for Education and the Director-General of the Ghana Education Service (GES) to put immediate and effective measures in place to reopen the school. He also called for appropriate safety arrangements to protect students when academic activities resume.

items.title: PANDEF mourns Uduaghan, hails his peacebuilding role
items.description: By Henry Umoru ABUJA — The Pan Niger Delta Forum (PANDEF), the apex socio-political body of the South-South geopolitical zone, has mourned the death of former Delta State Governor, Dr Emmanuel Uduaghan, who died three days before his 72nd birthday, according to his family. PANDEF National Chairman, Ambassador Godknows Igali, described Uduaghan as an exceptional leader whose commitment to the people of Delta State was unwavering. Igali stated this in a condolence letter to Delta State Governor, Sheriff Oborevwori, on the death of the former governor, according to a statement issued on Wednesday. He praised Uduaghan for his significant contributions to peace and stability in the Niger Delta, particularly during his tenure as Secretary to the State Government and later as governor, when militancy was heightened across the region. In the letter, Igali said he was shocked by the news of Uduaghan’s death, describing the late governor as a close associate and personal friend. “I write to express my total shock at the news of the passing into glory of our dearly beloved brother, the former Governor of Delta State, HE Dr Emmanuel Uduaghan. Although we mourn, but we all hold strong belief that the Almighty God knows best, and we glorify His exalted name,” he said. Igali added that he and Uduaghan had maintained a cordial relationship since they served simultaneously as secretaries to their respective state governments. “Without doubt, he was an exceptional man through and through, whose commitment to the people of Delta State was unfettered,” he said. He noted that Uduaghan played a significant role in bringing peace and stability to the Niger Delta during a period of heightened militancy in the South-South region. Igali described the former governor’s death as a major loss not only to Delta State but also to the Niger Delta and Nigeria as a whole. He expressed hope that Uduaghan’s legacy of service to God and humanity would endure, saying the late governor had “embedded his name in gold in the annals of our history.” Igali also asked Oborevwori to convey his deepest condolences to the Uduaghan family and the people of Delta State, praying for the repose of the former governor’s soul. items.title: Showunmi reaffirms commitment to Abiola’s legacy, national unity
items.description: By James Ogunnaike, Abeokuta The Convener of the Alternative Movement, Otunba Segun Showunmi has reaffirmed his commitment to Nigeria’s unity, democratic development and the ideals for which the late Chief Moshood Kashimawo Olawale (MKO) Abiola sacrificed his life, insisting that the struggle to actualise the June 12, 1993 presidential election mandate remains a defining moment in his political journey. Showunmi, in a statement titled “My Scar from MKO Abiola, My Sacrifice for Democracy, and My Unwavering Pan-Nigerian Conviction,” said the circumstances surrounding Abiola’s death and the annulment of the historic election had left an indelible mark on his life and political convictions. He also cautioned political actors against actions capable of undermining national stability, particularly the premature or unauthorised announcement of election results in ways that could trigger political tension and plunge the country into chaos. “The scar in my heart from the loss of Chief Moshood Kashimawo Olawale Abiola has not fully healed,” Showunmi said, adding that he would neither trivialise Abiola’s sacrifice nor pretend to be unfamiliar with the painful experiences that shaped Nigeria’s democratic struggle. He stressed that his remarks on the country’s political history had been misunderstood by some people, insisting that his intention was to caution against political conduct that could endanger peace, violate the law or destabilise the nation. Showunmi said his reference to the political events of 1992 was intended to illustrate the consequences of abandoning caution, restraint and respect for the law in the pursuit of political power. “I invoked the events of 1992 to illustrate how political situations can spiral out of control when caution, restraint and respect for the law are abandoned,” he said. He maintained that his intervention was intended as a warning about the potential consequences of political decisions, not an endorsement of reckless conduct. “My intervention was a warning about consequences, not an invitation to recklessness, and I will not permit reactionary forces to turn my counsel into something it was never intended to be,” he stated. According to him, political advice should be offered in the national interest, while individuals must ultimately decide whether to heed such counsel. He urged political contestants to consider the wider implications of their actions, warning that decisions taken without regard for the law and national stability could have far-reaching consequences for the country. Reaffirming his commitment to national unity, Showunmi declared that his political convictions were not driven by ethnic considerations and rejected any suggestion that he subscribed to the superiority of one ethnic group over another. “I must also state, unequivocally, that I am a Pan-Nigerian through and through. I have no interest in promoting the idea that one ethnic group is superior to another,” he said. He explained that his political philosophy was rooted in the collective dignity, security and prosperity of Nigerians, irrespective of their ethnic or regional backgrounds. Showunmi urged Yoruba activists and others who might disagree with his position to consider his statements within the broader context of his commitment to Nigeria’s unity. “My words and actions must be understood within the framework of my commitment to the Nigerian nation. I will not subordinate that commitment to ethnic sentiment, sectional advantage or the politics of exclusion,” he said. He added that his preference for national cohesion should not be interpreted as a lack of personal conviction or an inadequate understanding of the country’s political history. On Nigeria’s political future, Showunmi reiterated his support for a power-sharing arrangement under which the presidency would rotate between the northern and southern parts of the country. He argued that a predictable and mutually respected understanding of power rotation could help reduce political suspicion, strengthen national cohesion and promote democratic stability. “I have long expressed the view that Nigeria should manage political power through a pendulum arrangement between the Northern and Southern parts of the country,” he said. “In my considered opinion, a predictable and mutually respected understanding of power rotation offers a framework for reducing suspicion, strengthening national cohesion and sustaining our democratic journey.” He described the proposal as part of the broader need for political maturity, mutual understanding and an inclusive approach to managing Nigeria’s diversity. Paying tribute to Abiola, the presumed winner of the June 12, 1993 presidential election, which was annulled by the military government, Showunmi said the late politician’s legacy remained inseparable from Nigeria’s struggle for democratic governance. He prayed that Abiola’s sacrifice would continue to inspire Nigerians to work towards a more stable, just and enduring democracy. “May your supreme sacrifice continue to guide Nigeria towards a more stable, just and enduring democracy. May the promise for which you paid such a terrible price never be betrayed,” he said. Showunmi also disclosed that he intended to speak more extensively in the future about his personal contributions to the pro-democracy struggle and how the events surrounding Abiola shaped his political trajectory. “One day, God willing, I will speak more fully about my own contributions to the struggle for democracy,” he said. According to him, the experiences surrounding Abiola and the struggle to reclaim the June 12 mandate influenced his political outlook and redirected the course of his life, setting in motion developments whose consequences he said were still unfolding. He also acknowledged the role played by media entrepreneur and publisher Dele Momodu during that period, describing his contribution as significant to that chapter of Nigeria’s political history. “I must also acknowledge Dele Momodu. May God spare his life. He played a key and pivotal role in that chapter of our history, and his contribution deserves to be remembered,” Showunmi said. Showunmi warned against interpreting his restraint as a lack of knowledge of Nigeria’s democratic history or mistaking his commitment to national unity for an absence of personal convictions. “Finally, let nobody mistake my restraint for ignorance of history or my commitment to national unity for an absence of personal conviction,” he said. He added: “My commitment is to Nigeria. My loyalty is to the democratic ideal. My respect for MKO Abiola’s sacrifice is enduring. And my conviction that Nigeria must survive, mature and prosper remains unshaken.” “May God bless Nigeria and all who genuinely labour for her progress,” he said. The post Showunmi reaffirms commitment to Abiola’s legacy, national unity appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: Ferme géante Baladna d’Adrar : les trois objectifs majeurs de l’Algérie
items.description: La facture des importations réduite de 1,5 milliard de dollars par un seul projet : l’Algérie est en train de transformer le désert du Sahara en pôle agricole d'excellence et en pilier de sa souveraineté alimentaire. Les promesses de la ferme géante Baladna Algérie , implantée à Adrar, sont à la mesure de son gigantisme. Avec ce projet hors normes, l’Algérie poursuit trois objectifs majeurs : renforcer sa souveraineté alimentaire et faire du Sahara un pôle d’excellence agricole. Baladna Algérie : une production de 1,7 milliards de litres de lait à partir de fin 2027 Le projet intégré a reçu lundi 19 octobre la visite du ministre de l’Agriculture Sid Ali Khaldi qui a constaté sur place le taux satisfaisant de l’avancement des travaux : 80%. A ce rythme, la production de lait cru débutera à la fin de l’année 2027 et celle de lait en poudre début 2028. Le projet, fruit d’un investissement algéro-qatarie de 3,5 milliards de dollars, intègre la culture de fourrages à grande échelle, un élevage bovin de 240 000 vaches et une usine de production de poudre de lait. La capacité de production prévue est de 1,7 milliards de lait cru qui serviront à la production de 193 000 tonnes de poudre de lait par an, avec l'ambition stratégique de couvrir, à terme, 50 % des besoins nationaux de poudre de lait. Baladna Algérie : les premières génisses attendues fin novembre des États-Unis La superficie totale dédiée au projet est de 219 000 hectares. Le projet a également une dimension sociale avec la prévision de la création d’un total de 20 000 emplois. L’introduction des premières génisses, au nombre de 35 000, débutera fin novembre prochain. Elles seront importées des États-Unis. Les travaux vont bon train, a constaté le ministre, accompagné du wali d'Adrar et du président du conseil d'administration de Baladna El Djazaïr, Ali Al Ali. Au total, 102 lots ont été attribués, dont 69 % à des entreprises algériennes. Le projet mobilise actuellement 1 360 travailleurs. “Faire du Sud algérien un pôle d'excellence de l'investissement agricole” La ferme géante Baladna Algérie dynamisera aussi l'économie saharienne en développant la production locale de viande rouge et en favorisant un transfert technologique majeur pour l'agriculture nationale, indique l’entreprise. “Nous avons pour ambition de faire du Sud algérien un pôle d'excellence de l'investissement agricole, capable de valoriser les potentialités de la région et de soutenir le développement de filières agricoles intégrées”, a déclaré sur place le ministre Sid Ali Khaldi. “Ce que bâtit Baladna El Djazaïr aujourd'hui à Adrar constitue le socle de la sécurité alimentaire, en matière de lait, de toute l'Algérie pour les années à venir, où son engagement quotidien se résume en une promesse : Building today, feeding tomorrow (construire aujourd’hui, nourrir demain)”, a assuré pour sa part Ali Al Ali. L’article Ferme géante Baladna d’Adrar : les trois objectifs majeurs de l’Algérie est apparu en premier sur TSA .

items.title: La Tunisienne Amal Mekni parmi les 100 femmes héroïnes de la FAO
items.description: À travers son exploitation agricole, son engagement pour la valorisation des produits locaux et son action auprès des femmes en milieu rural, Amal Mekni incarne une agriculture tunisienne innovante, inclusive et durable. Sa reconnaissance par la FAO met en lumière le rôle moteur des femmes dans la transformation des systèmes agroalimentaires. De la région de Béja au siège de la FAO à Rome, le parcours d’Amal Mekni illustre la capacité des femmes à transformer les défis du monde rural en opportunités économiques et sociales. Ingénieure agronome et entrepreneure agricole tunisienne, elle figure parmi les 100 femmes héroïnes des systèmes agroalimentaires et du développement rural distinguées par l’Organisation des Nations Unies pour l’alimentation et l’agriculture (FAO), dans le cadre de l’Année internationale des agricultrices 2026. La cérémonie de reconnaissance s’est tenue le 15 octobre au siège de la FAO, à Rome, en marge du Forum mondial de l’alimentation. Cette distinction internationale salue des femmes dont le leadership, l’expertise et l’innovation contribuent à renforcer les systèmes agroalimentaires, à créer des opportunités pour les communautés rurales et à promouvoir un développement plus durable et inclusif. La sélection a été effectuée à l’issue d’un processus international ayant reçu 609 candidatures provenant de 131 membres de la FAO . De l’expertise agronomique à l’entrepreneuriat agricole À la tête de La Reine du Nord , une exploitation agricole située dans le gouvernorat de Béja, Amal Mekni a choisi de mettre ses compétences au service du développement agricole de sa région. Après une expérience dans l’industrie agroalimentaire, elle s’est engagée dans l’entrepreneuriat, avec l’ambition de valoriser les ressources locales et de développer une activité créatrice de valeur. Son projet s’inscrit dans une logique de valorisation des produits du terroir, notamment à travers l’élevage et la transformation laitière. Cette orientation avait déjà été mise en lumière par la FAO en 2021, lorsqu’Amal Mekni figurait parmi les jeunes entrepreneures accompagnées dans le cadre d’un programme consacré à l’investissement responsable des jeunes dans l’agriculture . Son projet portait alors sur l’élevage de brebis de race locale Thibar et la production de fromages de qualité, avec une ambition affirmée de valoriser les produits typiques du nord de Béja. Au-delà de la production, cette démarche illustre l’intérêt de rapprocher savoir-faire agronomique, transformation agroalimentaire et valorisation commerciale des produits locaux. Elle témoigne également du potentiel de l’entrepreneuriat agricole pour stimuler l’économie régionale et contribuer à la création d’activités et d’emplois en milieu rural. Un engagement qui dépasse les frontières de son exploitation La portée du parcours d’Amal Mekni réside aussi dans son engagement en faveur des autres femmes en milieu rural. Celle-ci préside un groupement de développement agricole féminin et accompagne une trentaine de femmes vers une plus grande autonomie économique. Elle contribue également au développement des compétences, avec plus de 100 stagiaires formés, et soutient des initiatives génératrices de revenus. Cette dimension collective donne une portée particulière à son engagement, car au-delà de la réussite d’une entreprise, il s’agit de favoriser l’accès des femmes aux compétences, de soutenir leurs initiatives économiques et de renforcer leur participation à la création de valeur dans les territoires ruraux. En mettant l’accent sur la valorisation des productions locales et l’autonomie économique des femmes, son expérience illustre une approche du développement rural dans laquelle l’innovation et la performance agricole peuvent aller de pair avec l’inclusion sociale. Mettre les femmes en milieu rural au premier plan La distinction accordée à Amal Mekni par la FAO dépasse la reconnaissance d’un parcours individuel. Elle contribue à rendre plus visibles les compétences, l’expertise et le leadership des femmes qui participent quotidiennement au fonctionnement des systèmes agroalimentaires, souvent sans bénéficier d’une reconnaissance à la hauteur de leur contribution. Cette mise en lumière prend un relief particulier en 2026, proclamée Année internationale des agricultrices par les Nations Unies. L’initiative vise notamment à sensibiliser à la contribution essentielle des femmes à l’agriculture , à la sécurité alimentaire et à la résilience économique, tout en attirant l’attention sur les inégalités qui limitent encore leur accès aux ressources, aux services et aux opportunités.. Pour la Tunisie, le parcours d’Amal Mekni constitue un exemple inspirant de la manière dont l’entrepreneuriat agricole peut contribuer à dynamiser les territoires, à valoriser les produits locaux et à ouvrir des perspectives économiques aux femmes rurales. D'après FAO . L’article La Tunisienne Amal Mekni parmi les 100 femmes héroïnes de la FAO est apparu en premier sur Kapitalis .

items.title: PAIDATA : le gouvernement et le FIDA lancent une mission conjointe de supervision
items.description: © DR Le ministre de l'Agriculture Gabriel Mbairobe a présidé le lundi 19 octobre 2026 à Yaoundé le lancement de la mission conjointe de supervision Gouvernement-FIDA du projet d'appui à l'intensification durable de l'agriculture et à la transition agroécologique. Accélérer avant la clôture de mars 2027. L'Administrateur du FODECC, M. Samuel Donatien Nengue, a pris part le lundi 19 octobre 2026 à la cérémonie de lancement de la mission conjointe de supervision Gouvernement-FIDA et d'appui à la mise en œuvre du PAIDATA. La cérémonie, présidée par le ministre de l'Agriculture et du Développement rural, M. Gabriel Mbairobe, s'est tenue dans la salle de conférence du MINADER à Yaoundé. La rencontre a réuni les représentants du MINEPAT, du MINFI, de la Caisse autonome d'amortissement, les responsables des directions du MINADER, ainsi qu'une importante délégation du Fonds international de développement agricole conduite par son directeur pays, M. Eric Rwabidadi. Les responsables du PAIDATA, de l'IRAD et d'autres projets bénéficiant des financements du FODECC étaient également présents. Prévue du 19 au 30 octobre 2026, cette mission a pour objectifs d'évaluer les performances du projet, d'examiner les réalisations techniques et financières, d'identifier les contraintes opérationnelles et de formuler des recommandations pour renforcer l'efficacité des interventions sur le terrain. À cette occasion, l'Administrateur du FODECC a présenté l'état d'avancement des diligences engagées pour satisfaire aux conditions de décaissement des ressources additionnelles du partenariat CAFI. Il a réaffirmé les efforts pour accélérer les procédures administratives et renforcer la justification des résultats, avec pour ambition de mobiliser les ressources disponibles avant la clôture du projet, prévue en mars 2027. Autre perspective majeure : la finance verte. M. Samuel Donatien Nengue a également évoqué les préparatifs liés à cette orientation stratégique, qui doit positionner le FODECC au cœur du financement de la transition agroécologique. Cet article PAIDATA : le gouvernement et le FIDA lancent une mission conjointe de supervision est apparu en premier sur Journalducameroun.com .

items.title: Hamzat mourns Afenifere leader Fasoranti, says legacy will endure
items.description: The Lagos State Deputy Governor, Dr. Obafemi Hamzat, has described the death of Pa Reuben Fasoranti, former National Leader of Afenifere, as a profound loss to the Yoruba race and Nigeria. Hamzat expressed his condolences in a message signed by Mr Tunde Alao, Senior Special Assistant to the Governor (Media), Office of the Deputy Governor, on Wednesday in Lagos. He extended his heartfelt sympathies, on behalf of his family, to the Fasoranti family, the government and people of Ondo State, and the entire Yoruba race over the death of the elder statesman at the age of 100. The deputy governor described Fasoranti as a distinguished educator, principled leader and respected voice in Nigeria’s socio-political landscape, whose life was devoted to justice, fairness and the preservation of Yoruba values within a united Nigeria. According to him, Fasoranti’s leadership of Afenifere reflected his unwavering commitment to the dignity, rights and aspirations of the Yoruba people. He said the late elder statesman’s courage, wisdom and steadfast adherence to principle earned him the respect of generations, making him a father figure, counsellor and custodian of enduring values in Yoruba leadership. “Pa Fasoranti lived a remarkable century of service to his people and humanity. His life was defined by integrity, conviction and an enduring commitment to justice. “He was a voice of wisdom whose counsel and principles will continue to inspire generations to come,” Hamzat said. The deputy governor noted that Fasoranti’s death was a significant loss not only to his immediate family and Ondo State but also to the Yoruba nation and Nigeria as a whole. He added that the late leader’s legacy of selfless service and principled leadership would remain a source of inspiration for generations to come. While acknowledging the grief occasioned by his death, the deputy governor urged the bereaved family and the Yoruba people to draw comfort from the enduring impact of Fasoranti’s life, the values he upheld and the many lives he touched. He prayed that Almighty God would grant the deceased eternal rest and give his family, loved ones and all those mourning his passing the strength and fortitude to bear the loss. (NAN) The post Hamzat mourns Afenifere leader Fasoranti, says legacy will endure appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: PSG : Kvaratskhelia, gravement blessé au genou droit, absent plusieurs mois
items.description: L'attaquant du PSG Khvicha Kvaratskhelia, blessé mardi contre le FC Barcelone, est « victime d'une rupture du ligament croisé antérieur du genou droit » et sera absent plusieurs mois, a annoncé mercredi le club. Ousmane Dembélé, blessé à la cuisse gauche, « restera en soins ces prochaines semaines » comme Marquinhos, touché à la cuisse droite, a précisé le PSG dans un communiqué médical, après la victoire (4-2) mardi à domicile face au Barça en Ligue des champions. Pour rappel, une semaine après avoir fait tomber Manchester City (4-2) sur sa pelouse, le PSG a enchaîné un troisième succès en autant de rencontres européennes en dominant 4-2 Barcelone mardi au Parc des Princes lors d'un choc spectaculaire en Ligue des champions. items.title: ‘Don’t treat it as an Obuasi episode’ – Kofi Asare calls for school safeguarding reforms
items.description: The Executive Director of Africa Education Watch, Kofi Asare, has called on the Ghana Education Service (GES), the Ministry of Education and the Ministry of Gender to use the sexual abuse scandal at Obuasi Senior High Technical School (SHTS) as an opportunity to reform safeguarding systems across the country. He said the allegations should not be treated as an isolated incident involving one school but as a wake-up call for a broader review of how sexual abuse complaints are handled and how students are protected in Ghanaian schools. Speaking on Joy FM’s Super Morning Show during a discussion on the Obuasi SHTS scandal, Mr Asare said the most important outcome should be lasting changes to the system rather than a response limited to the case. “For me, the most important thing in all this is that the GES, the Ministry of Education, and the Ministry of Gender; these three agencies should not see what is happening as an Obuasi episode,” he said. “No. We should see this as an opportunity to undertake system-wide reforms in safeguarding in Ghana.” Mr Asare acknowledged that scandals could occur in any country but said the response to such incidents determined whether institutions learnt from them and prevented similar cases in the future. He warned that treating the Obuasi case as an isolated incident would mean missing an opportunity to address weaknesses in the systems responsible for protecting students. “In every country, you know, scandals happen. But the most important thing is what countries, what nations make out of these scandals,” he said. “If we reduce it to a case, then we’ve lost it.” Mr Asare said one of the key reforms needed was to move safeguarding responses away from the direct control of the GES and place them under an external agency. He said that relying on the same institution to handle complaints and oversee responses could make it difficult to address persistent weaknesses in the system. He said Africa Education Watch had proposed an arrangement that would give an independent body responsibility for responding to safeguarding concerns in schools. “We should see this as a launchpad to undertake system-level reforms in safeguarding in our schools,” he said. He added that the proposed changes should include “feeding safeguarding responses to an external agency other than the GES system”. According to him, such a move would help address recurring problems instead of allowing the same issues to emerge repeatedly without meaningful reform. Mr Asare also welcomed the decision by the National Democratic Congress (NDC) to withdraw Zakaria Abdullahi from the party’s election in Juaben, but said this should have been taken without the need for sustained public pressure and advocacy. “I mean, the person has withdrawn. It is good,” he said. However, Mr Asare expressed concern that the decision came only after considerable pressure from campaigners and other concerned groups. “Unfortunately, it had to come on the back of strenuous advocacy and pressure. Well, we welcome the decision. But the standards for me are the most important for our democracy,” he said. He warned that Ghana was likely to encounter similar cases in the future, including situations involving people with political connections or links to political parties. “We will definitely meet similar cases in the future where people who are politically connected or politically associated persons participate in illegal activities in our school environment. Definitely, we will meet those cases,” he said. Mr Asare said the way political parties respond to such incidents would help establish standards for dealing with future cases. He said that taking a clear position when concerns first arise would make it easier for political parties and institutions to respond consistently when similar situations occur. “And so when you have good precedent, it makes it easier for the next incident to follow suit,” he said. While welcoming the NDC’s decision, Mr Asare said that the party should not have waited for public pressure before taking action. “But it shouldn’t have come on the back of pressure and advocacy. It should have been an easier decision to take in the interest of the parties,” he said.

items.title: Trump and Zelensky appear at loggerheads despite new optimism
items.description: The hug that Trump envoy Steve Witkoff offered Volodymyr Zelensky before talks in Oslo is unlikely to have dispelled the Ukrainian leader’s misgivings about the current direction of US policy towards his war-ravaged country. Zelensky posted a video of the moment on social media, with the message “Ukraine is working for peace. I thank our partners for their support!” But given everything that’s happened this month, does the Ukrainian leader still regard Donald Trump as a partner? The two men have never been close – that much is obvious – but have they now fallen out once and for all? Both in rhetoric and actions, the past 10 days have seen evidence of a rupture as deep as any in their fractious relationship. Just listen to the way they talk about each other. “Zelensky’s not a good guy for us to deal with,” Trump told Newsmax last week. The verbal assault has continued this week. “Zelensky doesn’t know what he’s talking about,” Trump told a reporter on Monday when asked what he thought of the Ukrainian leader’s suggestion that striking a diesel deal with Russia put the US on the wrong side of history. Such personal attacks are typical of Trump’s sledgehammer approach to diplomacy. It’s hard to know when to take them seriously. In June, he lashed out at Israel’s prime minister, saying Benjamin Netanyahu “has no f**king judgement”. Four months later, he endorsed Netanyahu enthusiastically, calling him a “great warrior prime minister”. “Trump can always do another U-turn,” says Ian Bond of the Centre for European Reform. “But this does look bad.” For his part Zelensky has generally been circumspect in how he describes his unreliable but vital American counterpart. But this month his frustration has been clear. Addressing a US congressional delegation, he spoke of “decisions on the American side that are hard to explain between friends” and voiced the fear that “some political decision has been made to slow down support for us.” Answering Trump’s charge that he represented the principal obstacle to a negotiated settlement, Zelensky sounded more exasperated than ever. “We have welcomed literally EVERY attempt by our partners to end this war with dignity,” he wrote on Telegram on Monday. But rhetoric aside, how bad is the relationship? In some ways, we’ve been here before. After their notorious televised bust up in the Oval Office in February 2025, at which Trump accused Zelensky of “gambling with World War III”, the US suspended military assistance and restricted intelligence sharing. The crisis only lasted a week. And when the Trump administration decided, later that year, that it no longer wanted to finance direct military assistance to Ukraine, a mechanism was put in place for European countries to pay for American equipment instead. One exception, in the wake of this year’s US war with Iran, has been badly needed US-made Patriot air defence missiles. Amid a global shortage, the supply to Ukraine has slowed to a trickle, making it harder than ever for Kyiv to shoot down Russian ballistic missiles. The Washington Post, quoting an unnamed Ukrainian official, said “only a couple” of Patriot interceptors remained in Ukraine’s stockpile, and that the Trump administration had slowed down the process by which US allies seek approval to transfer their stocks. Similar concerns have been voiced in the past, but the latest reports – not confirmed by US officials – come against an increasingly difficult backdrop for Kyiv. Earlier this month, as Ukrainian negotiators arrived in Miami for talks with Trump’s all-purpose envoys Witkoff and Jared Kushner, they were blindsided by the news that the president had just struck a deal with Vladimir Putin to open US markets to Russian diesel. Experts questioned whether it would do much to drive down US petrol prices, ahead of congressional mid-term elections (the apparent motive), but as a signal of US displeasure over Ukraine’s campaign of long-range strikes on Russian oil refineries and Washington’s willingness to do deals with the Kremlin, it represented a stinging rebuke to Kyiv. Last Friday, Trump went further, waiving wide-ranging sanctions on Russia just two days before they were due to take effect. Trump said the sanctions contained in the Graham Act (named after the former South Carolina senator Lindsey Graham, a vocal supporter of Ukraine who died in July) would hinder his efforts to broker peace. But for Kyiv and its supporters this was another alarming sign that the White House was siding with the Kremlin. “What the Trump administration is doing is providing carrots to the Russians and sticks to the Ukrainians,” former US ambassador to Kyiv William Taylor told the BBC. “It’s inexplicable and saddening.” Kiriil Dmitriev, a senior Putin envoy, called it “an important and truly historic moment”. For Moscow, this felt like a welcome return to the “spirit of Alaska”, a phrase much touted by Russian officials in the wake of the Trump-Putin summit in Anchorage in August 2025. Adding to the impression that Trump is turning his back on Ukraine is the allegation – again not confirmed by Washington – that the US has restricted the flow of intelligence and interfered with Ukraine’s access to Elon Musk’s Starlink satellite internet service. Amid an escalation in Russia’s drone and missile war on Ukraine’s cities, Kyiv says advance warning provided by US satellite intelligence has been lacking. “We didn’t receive it during ballistic attacks for three days,” Zelensky told NBC News. On 12 October five Russian S-400 missiles hit Kyiv, reportedly before air raid sirens or mobile alerts had sounded. The US Secretary of State, Marco Rubio, denied there had been any pause in intelligence sharing, blaming a “software problem” for the temporary lack of early warnings. Similar uncertainty surrounds Ukraine’s access to Starlink. A week ago, Ukrainian officials reported that the system was being throttled, with terminals unable to maintain connections at high speeds, making it harder for Ukraine’s military to intercept fast moving Russian drones. Since the summer, Ukraine has struggled to cope with a wave of attacks by advanced, jet-powered drones. It’s not clear where any order to limit Ukraine’s use of Starlink – or its military grade equivalent Starshield – originated. Reuters reported that it came from the White House. Rubio said “no-one at the White House ordered anyone to slow down internet.” But the fact that such suspicions surface so frequently points to the lack of trust that continues to infect US-Ukrainian relations. Much of this has its roots in Donald Trump’s seemingly long-standing mistrust of Ukraine as a whole – and Zelensky in particular. A decade ago, Trump became convinced that Ukraine had tried to prevent him from becoming US president. Among a number of unfounded allegations was the suggestion that the US Democratic National Committee had a server hidden somewhere in Ukraine. When Zelensky became president, three years later, he resisted Trump’s demands that he investigate charges of election interference. During a notorious July 2019 telephone conversation, Trump also asked Zelensky to investigate Joe Biden, the man who went on to defeat him in the 2020 presidential election. Again, Zelensky refused. At the time, the White House was withholding $391m (£290m) in military assistance to Ukraine, a juxtaposition that ultimately led to Trump’s first impeachment. Whether Trump’s resentment over these historic slights continues to inform his current policy towards Ukraine is an open question, but it’s clear that the roller coaster of US-Ukraine relations has taken another stomach-churning dip. Following the talks in Oslo, Witkoff is taking a set of updated proposals to St Petersburg. All eyes will now be on Putin. Jonas Gahr Støre, the Norwegian leader, said the talks in Oslo had helped “to straighten out a few things.” “There’s nothing to gain from… digging into what was said yesterday or a week ago,” he said diplomatically. Zelensky said the day had begun with a productive conversation with the US Secretary of State and indicated that the issue of early warning had already been fixed. He also sounded optimistic about Patriot missiles and Starlink. “I think we will have good results too,” he said. Yet despite the optimistic tone, it’s hard to get around the fact that Volodymyr Zelensky and Donald Trump appear, once again, to be at loggerheads.

items.title: Cameroun : la première journée mondiale de la santé environnementale célébrée à Yaoundé
items.description: © DR Célébrée pour la première fois le 19 octobre 2026 au Palais des Congrès de Yaoundé, la Journée mondiale de la santé environnementale a placé la science au cœur de la protection des communautés face à la pollution et à la dégradation des écosystèmes. Une première aux accents d'alerte. Le Cameroun a célébré pour la première fois, le 19 octobre 2026 au Palais des Congrès de Yaoundé, la Journée mondiale de la santé environnementale, sous le thème : "la santé environnementale : s'appuyer sur la science pour protéger les communautés". Habituellement célébrée le 26 septembre depuis 2011, cette journée vise à sensibiliser décideurs, professionnels et grand public au rôle déterminant de la santé environnementale dans la prévention des maladies. Au Cameroun, le lien est direct. La santé publique est impactée par la dégradation des écosystèmes, la gestion inappropriée des déchets et leur brûlage sauvage qui libère des toxines, la pollution de l'air à Douala et Yaoundé où les particules fines franchissent les seuils de sécurité, et l'insalubrité de l'eau. Les conséquences sont lourdes : maladies hydriques, affections respiratoires, prolifération des vecteurs. Les formations sanitaires reçoivent chaque jour enfants, mères et travailleurs souffrant de toux chronique, d'asthme sévère et d'infections aiguës causées par les émissions des transports et les poussières. Face à cela, le Gouvernement applique la stratégie "une seule santé". Parmi les actions concrètes : déploiement massif d'un réseau de surveillance de la qualité de l'air en temps réel via des stations fixes et mobiles, renforcement des contrôles et inspections environnementales, et soutien aux acteurs de terrain et municipalités à travers des initiatives de salubrité publique. Présidant la cérémonie, le Ministre de l'Environnement a appelé à la responsabilité de tous : collectivités, société civile, médias et secteur privé doivent respecter la législation environnementale. Aux citoyens, il a lancé un appel simple : "ne pas jeter d'ordures dans les drains, planter un arbre, préserver nos cours d'eau, l'arrêt définitif des feux de poubelles". Cet article Cameroun : la première journée mondiale de la santé environnementale célébrée à Yaoundé est apparu en premier sur Journalducameroun.com .

items.title: YEA trades and vocational programme exceeds 2026 target by 73% – Basintale
items.description: The Youth Employment Agency’s trades and vocational programme has recorded 51,900 beneficiaries against an annual target of 30,000, exceeding its target by 73%, Chief Executive Officer Malik Basintale has announced. Speaking at the Government Accountability Series at Jubilee House today, Wednesday, October 21, Mr Basintale said the programme was the Agency’s strongest-performing employment module by percentage as of September 30, 2026. The intervention provides young people with technical and vocational skills in areas such as carpentry, welding and hairdressing. It also supports beneficiaries who wish to establish small and medium-scale businesses by providing start-up tools. Mr Basintale said the performance demonstrated the importance of practical skills development and entrepreneurship in efforts to address youth unemployment. “Trades and Vocation module provides young people with technical and vocational skills across trade areas other than fashion,” he said, outlining the programme’s role in preparing beneficiaries for work and self-employment. He added: “Vocational skills are not inferior alternatives to formal jobs; they are essential pillars of productive economic participation.” The YEA says the programme is intended to help young people acquire practical competencies, establish businesses and participate in productive economic activities.

items.title: The Contradictions of Troy Jackson
items.description: The clouds, piled in a dark heap over the Blueberry Ridge mobile-home park in Wells, Maine, looked like they would open up any minute. Residents sat in neatly arranged folding chairs behind a double-wide trailer, waiting for Troy Jackson, the state’s Democratic Senate candidate, to appear. Meanwhile, campaign staffers buzzed around like hornets out of a nest, freshly kicked. I was seated at the periphery, flanked on the left by two pockmarked fake deer—3-D archery targets—and on the right by an elderly chain-smoker who politely angled her cigarette away from me as she talked. She told me that she didn’t know much about Jackson but was going to knock on doors for him anyway. “He seems like he’s down-to-earth,” she said. “That he’s one of us.” Jackson is one of them. He’s a fifth-generation logger born to a 16-year-old high-school dropout, and, as he is fond of repeating, he grew up as a “poor kid in a town full of poor kids.” At one time, he lived in a mobile home. A slick banner on his campaign website declares: Mainer By Birth. Logger By Trade. Senator for the People . I’d come to Blueberry Ridge to see Jackson, who replaced Graham Platner as the nominee in July, after Platner resigned due to multiple scandals. The park was bought by a real-estate-investment company in 2021, and a group of residents has claimed that the new owners have made life there more expensive and worse. Now the group is pushing for a rent cap, and Jackson was there over Labor Day weekend to show support. When he addressed the crowd, his voice was measured but tinged with what sounded like genuine frustration. “The greed that’s happening right now in this country, that people in mobile-home parks are feeling, is like something I’ve never seen,” he said. Jackson marveled at a mason jar of muddy tap water that got passed around, apparent evidence of the park’s deteriorating living conditions. He seemed to be in his element, and after the event was over, he stayed to shake hands and talk about the travails of mobile-home life until his staffers pulled him away. [ Read: One morning of controlled chaos in Maine ] The next stop on his tour that day was People’s Inclusive Welding, a school in South Portland whose mission is to provide a “safe and supportive environment for underserved and underrepresented communities to learn a skilled trade.” There, Jackson watched a torch demonstration, surrounded by the language of hyper-progressivism: a metal slab emblazoned with the text WHAT’S YOUR SAFE WORD? ; a door covered in dozens of stickers with radical messages ( SOLIDARITY MEANS WEARING A MASK and DESTROY ALL BORDERS ); a gigantic mural, painted the colors of the trans flag, proclaiming BLM and ACAB —an abbreviation for “All Cops Are Bastards.” He seemed to instinctively edge away from the mural as a local-news outlet snapped photos of him. The contrast between these two events—one at a trailer park populated mostly by retirees, the other at a shop catering to progressive urban tradespeople—reflects the tensions in the Jackson campaign as a whole. Jackson seems to be attempting to pair a left-leaning, economically populist package with “woke” cultural ideals, which working-class voters tend to reject. Jackson’s unsuccessful run for governor earlier this year was endorsed by the Democratic Socialists of America and Bernie Sanders, who affirmed his support for Jackson’s Senate bid and has appeared at campaign events on his behalf. Several labor unions have also endorsed Jackson. He supports Medicare for All, bans on congressional stock trading, tax cuts for workers, and tax hikes for billionaires. He also favors restricting assault weapons and abolishing ICE. As a state senator, he voted in favor of trans women being housed in women’s prisons, and of qualified trans teens receiving treatments such as hormone therapy without parental consent; he voted against a ban on trans women’s participation on women’s sports teams. In 2023, he co-sponsored legislation to allow later-term abortions after fetal viability. On economic issues, Jackson is in sync with the working-class and rural voters he says he is championing. Sixty-three percent of Americans without a college degree and 76 percent of those who make less than $50,000 a year say that the government should be responsible for ensuring health-care coverage, for example. On cultural matters, however, Jackson is out of step with many of those he claims to be giving a voice to. Most Americans without a college degree say that protecting gun rights is more important than gun control, and that guns make the country safer. These Americans are also more likely than college graduates to express negative views about illegal immigration. Likewise, a majority of people making less than $50,000 a year or who did not go to college say that abortion is morally unacceptable, whereas those making more than $100,000 or who did go to college say the opposite. On gender identity, majorities of Americans without a four-year college degree say that gender transitions are morally wrong, that trans people should play on sports teams that match their birth sex, and that being trans is not an innate condition but is instead caused by social factors. Similar trends play out in Maine, where people without a four-year college degree are more likely than people with a degree to view illegal immigration as a serious problem, and where trans women’s participation in women’s sports is unpopular across the electorate. (I asked the Jackson campaign for an interview so that he could elaborate on his views, but it refused multiple requests.) Despite its down-home signifiers and KICKING ASS FOR THE WORKING CLASS T-shirts, the Jackson campaign’s pairing of leftist economic populism with progressive cultural stances fits seamlessly into the broader professional-class insurgency roiling the Democratic Party. This movement, which some have referred to as a Democratic “tea party,” appears animated by a theory of persuasion that one might call “left maximalism.” The tacit wager of left maximalists, including Jackson, seems to be that enough working-class voters will stomach unpopular left-wing cultural policies provided that a candidate also supports popular left-wing economic positions. This strategy has shown some signs of success lately, as evidenced by the DSA-endorsed candidate Darializa Avila Chevalier’s surprise primary win in New York City’s Thirteenth Congressional District, one of the poorest in the state. She managed to unseat an incumbent establishment opponent despite arguing that deportations are wrong under any circumstance and that national borders and prisons should be abolished—views that are not exactly common among the working class. Similarly, before Platner’s collapse, he used a left-maximalist approach to win his primary. It remains to be seen, however, whether left maximalism will fly as a general-election strategy in Maine. Winning will require Jackson to hold together a coalition that includes both college-educated residents of prosperous coastal cities and towns, and the rural, socially moderate, working-class voters Democrats have been alienating in recent years. The frictions in the Jackson campaign’s platform call to mind the work of Daniel Bell, a mid-20th-century sociologist who once described himself as “a socialist in economics, a liberal in politics, and a conservative in culture.” In his 1976 book, The Cultural Contradictions of Capitalism , Bell argued that capitalism had started to undermine itself. As Bell observed, capitalism took root in the United States during the 19th and early-20th centuries, when the country’s social life was defined by puritanical moralism and the Protestant work ethic. Americans saved money, prioritized the public good, toiled mostly without complaint, and were disinclined to acquisitiveness. But after World War II, he wrote, thrift and public spiritedness were displaced by consumerist individualism, which focused on permissiveness, pleasure, and the self. Writing during a decade of economic crisis and high inflation, Bell warned that unfettered capitalism would weaken important institutions, cultural values, and social bonds—and ultimately lead to a society as unstable as it was selfish. If Bell was right to spotlight the “cultural contradictions of capitalism” in the 1970s, the cultural contradictions of anti-capitalism may well prove to be one of the most potent political conundrums of the 2020s: The American left has produced an environment that alienates many working-class people from candidates espousing economics designed to benefit them. [ Read: Why do rich kids love socialism? ] Jackson, apparently trying to manage these contradictions, is acting as though he can be everything to everyone. One minute, his team is launching a folksy ad , set at a backyard barbecue, about loggers paying more taxes than billionaires. The next minute, the campaign is dropping a side-eye-emoji’d social-media clip of the candidate sassily sipping boba tea beside a Pride flag. Depending on your perspective, this mishmash is reflective either of a politician who is trying to represent all Mainers, or of a man whose cultural politics sit uneasily alongside those of the working-class electorate—not to mention his own past beliefs. When Jackson first (and unsuccessfully) ran for state office in 2000, he did so as a Republican . By 2002, he was an independent, and by 2004, a Democrat. Yet even after changing his party affiliation, he voted against same-sex-marriage legislation in 2009, and received a perfect score from an anti-abortion group, Maine Right to Life, in 2010. By 2017, though, Jackson had done an about- face . He eventually began receiving accolades from pro-choice organizations for his support of abortion rights. Jackson, who was raised Catholic, has described abortion as an issue he has long wrestled with, and has said that he was simply persuaded that his prior views were wrong. It is more than possible that Jackson’s pivot did come from a sincere change of heart, rather than from a cynical calculation about the concessions necessary to succeed as a Democrat. And the mixed messages of Jackson’s current campaign are not irreconcilable. Jackson can court the Rural Flannel-Wearing Tree Cutters and the Urban Boba Wokes at the same time, and perhaps he really will win enough of each for the Maine electoral math to work out in the Democrats’ favor. Polling shows a tight race, and the Iran quagmire, Donald Trump’s subbasement approval rating, and rising heating-oil prices in advance of the Maine winter are unlikely to do his opponent, the five-term Republican incumbent Susan Collins, any favors. But what may work as a matter of immediate tactics is not necessarily a strategy for fundamentally reshaping the demographics of the Democratic Party within the state, or outside it. Cultural politics, not economic politics, are the left’s primary barrier to winning back the working class. Left maximalists tend to treat the working class as a junior partner rather than as their primary constituency. Progressive urban professionals may get the economic and social politics they want, while rural and working-class voters are asked to compromise their moral and cultural belief system in exchange for promises of health care and an increased minimum wage. [ Read: The blockbuster that captured a growing American rift ] After Jackson departed Blueberry Ridge, I stuck around the backyard to talk with some residents. One was a union tinsmith and lifelong Democrat who told me he doesn’t care about culture-war issues and is more worried about how labor is being fleeced. Another was a tollbooth worker and three-time Trump voter who was dismayed that the president he’d voted for had done so little for the little people. He seemed ready for something different, and sympathized with Troy Jackson’s anti-corporate politics, but said that he could never vote for Jackson because of his stances on immigration and gender issues. Progressives may wonder why a Mainer whose trailer park is allegedly being wrecked by an investment firm would care more about immigration policy than affordability issues as he decides which candidate to support. But one could also ask the opposite question: Why are highly educated leftists, and politicians such as Jackson who appeal to them, often unwilling to give even an inch on social issues? If socialists and populists—even blue-collar leftists such as Jackson—are so wedded to progressivism that they do not compromise with the working class, the question is not simply whether such a left can win. The question is whether it truly remains left at all.

items.title: Canadian Officers Don’t Want to Serve in the U.S. Anymore
items.description: T he shortest flight path from Russia to the United States would take an enemy bomber over the North Pole and across Canadian airspace. During the Cold War, that simple fact was the impetus for the creation of the North American Aerospace Defense Command, or NORAD, which forged an integrated radar network across the two countries, effectively treating North American airspace as a single defensive zone. Today, there’s less concern about a Russian barrage landing on U.S. soil, but NORAD remains relevant. Russian bombers still fly near Alaska and the Canadian Arctic. China’s expanding nuclear arsenal poses its own threat. Other airborne objects require vigilance, a lesson underscored by the mysterious flight path, in 2023, of a Chinese spy balloon, which NORAD shot down. This should matter to President Trump, who has identified the Western Hemisphere as a security priority. He even has a name for his approach: the “Donroe Doctrine.” But all is not well at NORAD, the world’s only binational military command, headquartered at the Peterson Space Force Base in Colorado Springs. NORAD, which was founded in 1958, now demonstrates how the president’s disdain for U.S. allies risks undermining the military cooperation that has kept the United States safe for decades. Positions at NORAD and other integrated combatant commands in the United States used to be plum posts for ambitious Canadian military officers, giving them a chance to coordinate with Americans on intelligence, air and missile defense, and joint operations. That’s changing. U.S. and Canadian officials told me that Canada has lately struggled to find senior officers willing to take the jobs, a problem acute enough that Canadian officers have shared their concerns with counterparts in Colorado Springs, Ottawa, and Washington. The reasons are threefold, according to current and former officials who described the dynamic to me on the condition of anonymity in order to address a sensitive subject. Although the influence and sophistication of the U.S. military once made the postings desirable to ambitious officers, some now fear that time in the United States might hurt their chances for future promotions if relations spiral further out of control. They also see diminishing returns from a posting in which they’re likely to have their access curtailed as a byproduct of political tensions. And they face resistance from their families, who worry that anti-Canadian sentiment whipped up by Trump might make the country inhospitable, even temporarily. Canadian officers considering U.S.-based posts don’t believe that they’ll be treated as equals, according to several who spoke with me. While the Trump administration has bullied and threatened numerous allies, these officers perceive particular hostility toward Canada—in part because of the vehemence of the trade dispute, and in part because Prime Minister Mark Carney has been willing, at times, to stand up to Trump. “If you’re a two-star general in Canada, and you’ve got maybe one or two extremely important jobs left in your career, will you use one of them to take up a position in the States, where you might be underemployed, with little access and little meaningful work to show for it?” one Canadian officer asked. [ Read: Trump is learning that his bullying has consequences ] Some of the officials I spoke with noted that strained relations had not yet caused a tactical breakdown—no one had taken their eye off radar scopes or infrared cameras. And that’s what a NORAD spokesperson emphasized in response to my questions, issuing a statement saying that high-level Canadian roles at the binational command “remain fully staffed and highly regarded as career-enhancing opportunities, with Canadian personnel and their families fully integrated and operating with the systemic access required to execute binational defense operations for the homelands.” The true impact of Canadian reluctance to serve in the United States may become manifest only in a crisis. In addition to the essential national-security functions performed by NORAD, the command also fosters camaraderie between the ranks of the two militaries. That’s vital if the U.S. military should ever need to project force to the north, including by moving personnel across Canada. Several of the people I spoke with raised the prospect of a conflict with China, which would quickly threaten Alaska, a crucial strategic hub. Moving U.S. forces to the noncontiguous state would depend on Canadian cooperation. In such a situation, Washington would want Canadian commanders who have served in the United States, so that American officers aren’t building new partnerships but are depending on people they’ve known for years. Canadian generals who’ve passed on postings in the United States because of friction between the two countries are much less likely to be sympathetic. S ince he returned to power last year , Trump has alienated longtime allies while praising rogue states such as North Korea. He has called Germany a “broken country” and said that French President Emmanuel Macron “always gets it wrong.” As a group, European leaders earned the epithet “weak.” He has imposed steep tariffs on their countries and threatened a foundation of Western security by raising doubts about U.S. fidelity to Article 5 of the NATO charter—that an attack on one is an attack on all. Still, when I speak with senior officers in various allied countries—even Denmark , where the armed forces prepared for a possible U.S. invasion of Greenland, earlier this year—they maintain that military-to-military cooperation continues despite political disagreements. Canada may be the first place where that is cracking. “The day-to-day relationship has deteriorated,” David Perry, an Ottawa-based defense analyst, told me. “There’s been a tangible change in the way the two countries interact on defense and security.” That Washington is now choosing to alienate its northern neighbor is ironic because Canada, like other NATO members, is in the process of investing in the type of hard power that will make it an even more useful ally. When I met with Canada’s defense minister, David McGuinty, in February, the government had just released its first defense–industrial strategy, a plan to get weapons faster and—given geopolitical strife—to get more of them from Canadian suppliers. “Obviously continuing to work with the U.S.,” McGuinty said, “but now much more expansively looking to diversify.” Earlier this year, the Canadian government promised to review whether to move forward with a full order of F-35 stealth fighters, which are produced by Lockheed Martin. This month, the government paused its acquisition of U.S.-made Black Hawk helicopters because of trade and diplomatic friction with Washington, according to CBC News and Radio-Canada. Canada is spending billions to upgrade radars, sensors, and other systems. Its participation in Trump’s proposed “Golden Dome” would extend and strengthen the defensive shield, with the potential to protect both countries. But it’s hard to put much faith in protection from a bully. “Trust is easy to lose and hard to build,” Christopher Sands, the director of the Center for U.S.-Canada Studies at Johns Hopkins University School of Advanced International Studies, told me. The current rancor is entirely different from past trade disputes, which have often been combative—“like a courtroom drama,” Sands said. But the fighting once stayed out of public view, managed by low-profile diplomats. Now the public is in the audience and can’t look away from the president’s antics, which have “poisoned people-to-people relations.” The armed forces couldn’t remain immune forever. A n executive order on Trump’s first day back in office, in January 2025, made Canadian officers wonder whether the U.S. military might be used against them. The order assigned U.S. Northern Command, which shares NORAD’s Colorado headquarters, to the mission to “seal the borders and maintain the sovereignty, territorial integrity, and security of the United States.” It did not specify the southern border, causing Canadian officials in Colorado to ask their counterparts, as relations worsened over time: Are you planning to militarize the northern border, one of the world’s longest undefended and peaceful frontiers? U.S. officials tried to reassure them that any action would be cooperative. But the guarantee of cooperation became difficult to sustain. Defending new tariffs imposed on Canada in February 2025, Trump wrote on social media that “Canada ceases to exist as a viable Country” without U.S. support. “Therefore, Canada should become our Cherished 51st State.” Early on, references to Canadian statehood had elicited laughs during staff meetings at NORAD. But the mood soon changed. In April, Trump rebuffed the suggestion that his talk of annexation was just bluster. “I’m really not trolling,” he said in an interview with Time . By the end of the year, jokes within the binational command about the 51st state were met with silence or curt rebuttals. Attitudes had shifted dramatically. An Angus Reid Institute poll found that almost half of Canadians said that their government should view the United States as an “enemy” or “potential threat,” while only 27 percent called Washington a friend and ally. Canadian officers serving in the United States divulged to colleagues that their families didn’t want to visit them over the holidays, because they were afraid of crossing the border or encountering animosity in American communities. In addition to the joint command in Colorado Springs, Canadian generals have served as deputy commanders of U.S. Army corps in North Carolina, Texas, and Washington State. In early 2026, Carney named the dynamic generated by Trump’s hostility to American allies. “We are in the midst of a rupture,” he said, calling on the world’s middle powers to band together to resist bullying and defend international institutions. (Later, in an interview with The New York Times , Carney said that it would have been “irresponsible” not to take into consideration the possibility that Trump might use force against Canada.) [ Watch: How did Trump’s trade fight with Canada go so sideways? ] The president’s insults might have been dismissed as a rhetorical feint—a way to demand better trading terms or shake loose more military spending—but the scorn for Canada was echoed by senior Pentagon leaders. In May, Elbridge Colby, the undersecretary of defense for policy, used social media to complain about Canada’s military readiness and announce that the Trump administration was pausing its participation in the Permanent Joint Board on Defense, a bilateral advisory body to coordinate security policy. “A strong Canada that prioritizes hard power over rhetoric benefits us all,” Colby wrote. “Unfortunately, Canada has failed to make credible progress on its defense commitments.” The board hadn’t met since 2024, so the move was mostly symbolic. But Colby’s withering review prompted nervous questions inside NORAD: Who is this guy, and how much power does he have? Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth’s approach was even less subtle. In August, he posted a photo of two young female Canadian cadets. Their physical appearance seemed not to impress him; he captioned the photo “this is real.” The post stunned Canadians for its crassness and unprofessionalism. Wayne Eyre, who served as chief of Canada’s defense staff from 2021 to 2024, told me that he found Hegseth’s intervention “highly insulting.” It was followed, the next month, by a cartoon image that Trump circulated on his Truth Social feed of him beating Carney with a hockey stick—“unimaginable conduct by the president of the United States, even in our most dystopian imagination,” as one Canadian official put it to me. U.S. military leaders at NORAD have tried to put on a brave face, reporting to visitors that binational cooperation is continuing unimpeded. But away from the spotlight, Canadian officers will acknowledge the strain, current and former officials told me. Eyre warned that cooperation of the kind that he helped oversee is more vulnerable than it might appear. “It’s sad, disappointing, and disturbing to see that deep relationship come under attack,” he said. “In my view, it’s a case of the U.S. undergoing self-harm by discarding and calling into question its competitive advantage, which is this system of alliances.” Most of what the public knows about NORAD comes from its Santa Tracker , a lighthearted simulation of Santa Claus’s journey around the world on Christmas Eve. That’s because the command’s real business—guarding the skies—is mostly invisible. That is, until it stops working.

Coopération Camerou-Royaume Uni : le MINPMEESA mobilise de nouveaux partenariats pour la filière bois
items.description: © DR Le ministre Achille Bassilekin III a reçu le conseiller principal forêts du Royaume-Uni, Neil Scotland. Au menu : transformation locale du bois, développement des PME forestières et valorisation durable des ressources, avec en vitrine le SMEs Wood's Park de Lomié. Yaoundé veut verdir sa diplomatie économique. Le Ministre des Petites et Moyennes Entreprises, de l'Économie Sociale et de l'Artisanat, Achille Bassilekin III, a accordé une audience à M. Neil Scotland, Conseiller principal pour les forêts au ministère britannique des Affaires étrangères, du Commonwealth et du Développement (FCDO). Il était accompagné de Mme Samantha Smith, Haut-Commissaire adjointe et Chargée d'Affaires, et de M. Euan McCarthy, Conseiller régional en climat et environnement pour l'Afrique centrale. Au cœur des échanges : le renforcement de la coopération bilatérale en faveur de la transformation locale du bois, du développement des PME forestières, de la modernisation des équipements, du transfert de technologies et de la mobilisation de financements adaptés aux entreprises camerounaises. Une priorité pour le gouvernement camerounais qui entend faire de la valorisation responsable des ressources forestières un levier de croissance, de compétitivité et de développement durable. Cette dynamique trouve une illustration concrète dans le SMEs Wood's Park de Lomié, dont la convention de partenariat entre le MINPMEESA et la Commune de Lomié a été signée le 6 octobre 2026. Ce projet vise à favoriser le développement des PME, des artisans et des organisations de l'économie sociale, tout en stimulant la création d'emplois et la production de biens à plus forte valeur ajoutée. À travers ces perspectives de coopération, le MINPMEESA entend affirmer son crédo : pour des PME plus compétitives et une transformation locale créatrice de valeur, au bénéfice des entreprises et de l'économie nationale. Cet article Coopération Camerou-Royaume Uni : le MINPMEESA mobilise de nouveaux partenariats pour la filière bois est apparu en premier sur Journalducameroun.com .

items.title: Tour du Faso 2026 : Dix étapes, huit régions et une quinzaine de nations au départ
items.description: La 37e édition du Tour international cycliste du Faso se tiendra du 30 octobre au 8 novembre 2026. À quelques jours du début de la course, le comité d'organisation a rendu public, ce mercredi 21 octobre 2026, le circuit qui se décline en dix étapes traversant huit régions du Burkina Faso. Les régions concernées sont le Kadiogo, le Koulsé, le Nando, le Bankui, le Guiriko, le Nakambé, le Nazinon et l'Oubri. Le parcours s'ouvre le 30 octobre avec la première étape, Ouagadougou-Kaya. La deuxième mène les coureurs de Ouagadougou à Koudougou, avant la troisième, Koudougou-Boromo. La quatrième étape se dispute sur un circuit fermé à Bobo-Dioulasso, puis la cinquième relie Bobo-Dioulasso à Pâ. La sixième étape conduira le peloton de Saponé à Léo, la septième de Ouagadougou à Pô, et la huitième de Ouagadougou à Koupéla. La neuvième étape mènera de Tenkodogo à Ziniaré, avant l'arrivée finale, le 9 novembre, entre Dapélogo et Ouagadougou. Le Burkina Faso, pays hôte, alignera trois équipes : une sélection nationale et deux équipes régionales. Au total, 21 coureurs burkinabè ont été retenus. Toutes les équipes ont confirmé leur participation. 13 formations prendront part à cette édition 2026 : le Burkina Faso, le Mali, le Niger, la Belgique, le Maroc, le Ghana, le Bénin, le Cameroun, la Côte d'Ivoire, les Pays-Bas, l'Algérie, le Rwanda et l'Afrique du Sud.
